notes.summary: Biology gives about 2 questions per paper. Past papers ask most about plant and animal kingdoms, the human body, cells, diseases with their causes, vitamins and plant processes. Many questions are 'odd one out' or 'which pair is wrong', so learn each fact with its group: bacterial or viral disease, fat- or water-soluble vitamin, which phylum.

concepts.title: The cell
concepts.body:
• Robert Hooke (1665) saw cells in cork (dead cells). Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells such as bacteria. Robert Brown found the nucleus (1831).
  • Cell theory: Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals), 1838 to 1839; Rudolf Virchow added that new cells come from existing cells (1855).
  • Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae) have no nuclear membrane. Eukaryotes have a true nucleus.
  • The cell membrane follows the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).
  • Largest cell: ostrich egg. Longest cell: nerve cell. Smallest cell: mycoplasma (PPLO). Mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus.
OrganelleJob
NucleusControl centre; holds DNA
Mitochondria'Powerhouse': cellular respiration, makes ATP; has its own DNA
ChloroplastPhotosynthesis (plants only)
RibosomeProtein synthesis (no membrane)
Endoplasmic reticulumRough ER makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids
Golgi apparatusPacks and sends materials (Camillo Golgi)
Lysosome'Suicide bags': digest waste and worn-out parts
VacuoleStorage; large in plant cells
Cell wallPlants (cellulose), fungi (chitin); absent in animal cells
CentrosomeCell division in animal cells

concepts.title: Cell division and tissues
concepts.body:
• Mitosis: one cell gives two identical cells (growth, repair). Walther Flemming stained and described chromosomes in mitosis (1882).
  • Meiosis: makes gametes; halves the chromosome number; four cells.
  • Plant tissues: meristematic (dividing; at tips: apical, sides: lateral, nodes: intercalary) and permanent (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma). Xylem carries water up; phloem carries food.
  • Animal tissues: epithelial (covering), connective (blood, bone, cartilage; ligament joins bone to bone, tendon joins muscle to bone), muscular (striated voluntary, smooth involuntary, cardiac), nervous (neurons).

concepts.title: Genetics
concepts.body:
• Gregor Mendel, the father of genetics, worked with pea plants (laws of dominance, segregation and independent assortment).
  • DNA double helix: Watson and Crick (1953), helped by Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images. DNA bases: adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine; RNA has uracil instead of thymine.
  • Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes). Women XX, men XY, so the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.
  • Disorders: Down syndrome (an extra chromosome 21), Turner syndrome (XO), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), haemophilia and colour blindness (X-linked, more common in men), sickle-cell anaemia, thalassaemia. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A comes from a duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17.
  • Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003.
  • Hugo de Vries proposed the mutation theory; Darwin proposed natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859); Lamarck proposed use and disuse.

concepts.title: Classification and scientific names
concepts.body:
• Carl Linnaeus: father of taxonomy; binomial nomenclature (genus + species).
  • Whittaker's five kingdoms (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Viruses are not placed in any kingdom.
  • Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead matter (detritus) into simple inorganic substances.
  • Plant groups: algae (thallophyta); bryophytes like mosses ('amphibians of the plant kingdom'); pteridophytes like ferns (first with vascular tissue); gymnosperms with naked seeds (pine, cycas); angiosperms with flowers and fruit (monocots and dicots).

concepts.body:

PlatyhelminthesFlatworms; mostly parasitesTapeworm, liver fluke
NematodaRoundwormsAscaris, hookworm, filarial worm
AnnelidaSegmented bodyEarthworm, leech
ArthropodaJointed legs, hard outer skeleton; the largest phylumInsects, spiders, crabs, prawns, centipedes

Vertebrate classHeart chambers and features
Fish (Pisces)2 chambers; gills; cold-blooded
Amphibians3 chambers; live on land and in water (frog, toad, salamander)
Reptiles3 chambers (crocodile has 4); scaly skin
Birds (Aves)4 chambers; warm-blooded; feathers, hollow bones
Mammals4 chambers; warm-blooded; hair, milk glands
  • Whale, dolphin and bat are mammals. Platypus and echidna are mammals that lay eggs. Seahorse is a fish; starfish, jellyfish and silverfish are not fish.
  • A butterfly goes through complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), adult. So the third stage is the pupa.

concepts.title: Plant life processes
concepts.body:
• Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 (glucose) + 6O2, using sunlight and chlorophyll. The oxygen released comes from water. Light reactions occur in the grana, dark reactions (Calvin cycle) in the stroma. Glucose is stored as starch.
  • Transpiration: water loss through stomata; it pulls water up the xylem.
  • Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes (pea, gram); Azotobacter free in soil; blue-green algae (Anabaena) in rice fields.
  • Tropisms: phototropism (to light), geotropism (to gravity), hydrotropism (to water), thigmotropism (to touch, tendrils). The touch-me-not plant (Mimosa) folds its leaves on touch.
  • Parthenocarpy: fruit develops without fertilisation (seedless fruits).
  • Vegetative propagation: potato (stem tuber), ginger (rhizome), onion (bulb), Bryophyllum (leaf buds).
  • Insect-eating plants (pitcher plant, Venus flytrap, sundew) grow in nitrogen-poor soil. Cuscuta (amarbel) is a parasite.
  • Largest flower: Rafflesia. Smallest flowering plant: Wolffia. J.C. Bose invented the crescograph to measure plant growth.
Plant hormoneMain role
AuxinGrowth at shoot tips; bending towards light
GibberellinStem lengthening, seed germination
CytokininCell division; delays ageing
Abscisic acidStress hormone; closes stomata, causes dormancy
EthyleneGas that ripens fruit

concepts.title: Human organ systems
concepts.body:
• Digestion: saliva (amylase digests starch); stomach (hydrochloric acid and pepsin for proteins); liver makes bile (emulsifies fat; stored in the gall bladder); pancreas gives trypsin, lipase and amylase; most digestion and absorption happen in the small intestine (villi); the large intestine absorbs water.
  • Respiration: gas exchange in the alveoli of the lungs. Muscles under heavy exercise respire without enough oxygen and make lactic acid, which causes cramps and soreness.
  • Circulation (William Harvey, 1628): the heart has 4 chambers. The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood back. The SA node is the natural pacemaker.
  • Blood: RBCs carry oxygen (haemoglobin, which needs iron; myoglobin in muscle also needs iron); WBCs fight infection; platelets help clotting. Blood groups were found by Karl Landsteiner (1900). O negative is the universal donor; AB positive the universal recipient.
  • Excretion: kidneys filter blood; the nephron is the unit. Urea is made in the liver.
  • Nervous system: cerebrum (thinking, memory; largest part), cerebellum (balance and posture), medulla oblongata (heartbeat, breathing, involuntary acts). Reflex actions are controlled by the spinal cord. Serotonin, a neurotransmitter for mood and sleep, is made from the amino acid tryptophan.
GlandHormone and role
Pituitary ('master gland')Growth hormone and hormones that control other glands
ThyroidThyroxine (needs iodine; lack causes goitre)
ParathyroidControls blood calcium
AdrenalAdrenaline ('fight or flight')
Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it
PinealMelatonin (sleep cycle)
ThymusImmunity (T cells)
Testes; ovariesTestosterone; oestrogen and progesterone

concepts.title: Nutrition and vitamins
concepts.body:
Nutrients: carbohydrates and proteins give about 4 kcal per gram, fats about 9 kcal per gram. Proteins build the body. Casimir Funk coined the word 'vitamine' (1912).

VitaminChemical nameDeficiency diseaseSources
ARetinolNight blindness, xerophthalmiaCarrot, milk, fish-liver oil
B1ThiamineBeriberi (the first B vitamin found, from Eijkman's work in 1897)Whole grains
B2RiboflavinCracked lips and mouth cornersMilk, eggs
B3NiacinPellagraGroundnut, meat
B9Folic acidAnaemia; birth defectsGreen leafy vegetables
B12Cobalamin (has cobalt)Pernicious anaemiaMeat, milk
CAscorbic acidScurvy (bleeding gums)Amla, citrus fruits
DCalciferolRickets (children), osteomalacia (adults)Sunlight, fish oil
ETocopherolReproductive problemsVegetable oils, nuts
KPhylloquinoneBlood does not clot; excessive bleedingGreen leafy vegetables
  • Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K. Water-soluble: B and C. Vitamin C is destroyed by heat.
  • Minerals: iron (anaemia), iodine (goitre), calcium (bones and teeth), fluorine (teeth; too much causes fluorosis).
  • Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency. Marasmus: deficiency of both protein and calories.

concepts.title: Diseases and their causes
concepts.body:
CauseDiseases
BacteriaTuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, plague, leprosy, pneumonia, anthrax, botulism, syphilis, gonorrhoea
VirusesCommon cold, influenza, measles, mumps, chickenpox, smallpox, polio, rabies, hepatitis B, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, AIDS, COVID-19
ProtozoaMalaria (Plasmodium), amoebic dysentery (Entamoeba), kala-azar (Leishmania), sleeping sickness (Trypanosoma)
FungiRingworm, athlete's foot, candidiasis
WormsFilariasis (elephantiasis), ascariasis, tapeworm infection
VectorDisease
Female Anopheles mosquitoMalaria
Aedes aegypti mosquitoDengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever
Culex mosquitoFilariasis, Japanese encephalitis
SandflyKala-azar
Tsetse flySleeping sickness
Rat fleaPlague
HouseflyCarries typhoid, cholera germs on its body
  • Tests: Widal (typhoid), ELISA (HIV), Mantoux (tuberculosis).
  • Vaccines: Edward Jenner made the smallpox vaccine (1796); Louis Pasteur the rabies vaccine (1885); BCG protects against tuberculosis; Jonas Salk made the injected polio vaccine and Albert Sabin the oral one. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980; India was declared polio-free in 2014.
  • Robert Koch found the tuberculosis germ (1882) and the cholera germ. Ronald Ross showed mosquitoes spread malaria (1897). Quinine (from cinchona bark) treats malaria.
  • Organs: hepatitis and jaundice affect the liver; tuberculosis and pneumonia mainly the lungs; meningitis the coverings of the brain; goitre the thyroid; diabetes mellitus is linked to insulin from the pancreas.
  • Sexually transmitted diseases can be bacterial (syphilis, gonorrhoea) or viral (HIV/AIDS, genital herpes, hepatitis B).

varieties.name: Cell, tissues and genetics
varieties.how: Learn one job per organelle and which ones only plants have (cell wall, chloroplast, large vacuole). For genetics, learn chromosome numbers and the disorder table.

example.q: Which organelle is called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
steps: Energy (ATP) is made during cellular respiration.

varieties.name: Classification of living things
varieties.how: Place the organism in its phylum or class by its key feature: spiny skin and tube feet (echinoderm), jointed legs (arthropod), milk glands (mammal).

example.q: Which group of animals has spiny skin and a water-driven tube system for moving?
steps: Their water vascular system works the tube feet (starfish, sea urchin).

varieties.name: Plant life processes
varieties.how: Know the photosynthesis equation and where each step happens, the five hormones with one role each, and the special terms (parthenocarpy, tropisms).

example.q: The development of fruit without fertilisation is called:

varieties.name: Human body
varieties.how: Learn the key numbers table, then each organ system's main parts. For glands, link gland, hormone and disorder.

example.q: Insulin is produced by which organ?
steps: It is made by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.

varieties.name: Nutrition and vitamins
varieties.how: Learn vitamin, chemical name and disease in one line. Split them into fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B, C).

example.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes excessive bleeding from wounds?
steps: Its lack means wounds keep bleeding.

varieties.name: Diseases and pathogens
varieties.how: First decide the type of germ (bacterium, virus, protozoan, fungus, worm). Then recall the vector and the test or vaccine.

steps: Malaria is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.
The germ is Plasmodium, a protozoan.

varieties.name: Biologists, discoveries and branches
varieties.how: Pair each scientist with one discovery, and each '-logy' with its subject.

example.q: Who discovered the first vaccine, against smallpox?
steps: Pasteur made rabies and anthrax vaccines later.
Edward Jenner made the smallpox vaccine in 1796.

tips: Fat-soluble vitamins: 'ADEK'. All others (B, C) dissolve in water.
Heart chambers climb with class: fish 2, amphibians 3, most reptiles 3, birds and mammals 4.
Mosquito hook: Anopheles for malaria, Aedes for dengue (A-D), Culex for filariasis.
Ligament links bone to bone; tendon ties muscle to bone.
Five kingdoms in order of complexity: 'My Pet Frog Plays Ants' (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia).
Bones: 206 in adults, femur longest, stapes smallest.
traps: Malaria is caused by a protozoan, not a virus or bacterium; dengue is viral.
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, unlike other arteries.
Whale and bat are mammals; seahorse is a fish; starfish is not a fish.
Night blindness is vitamin A, but scurvy is vitamin C and rickets is vitamin D.
Robert Hooke saw dead cork cells; Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

questions.q: Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.solution:
Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and produce energy as ATP.
Memory hook: Mighty-chondria = the mighty power plant.

questions.q: Night blindness is caused by deficiency of:
questions.solution:
Vitamin A is needed for the light-sensitive pigment in the retina; its lack causes night blindness. Carrots are a good source.
Memory hook: A for 'Aankh' (eye).

questions.q: How many bones are there in the body of an adult human?
questions.solution:
An adult has 206 bones. A newborn has about 300; many fuse as the child grows.
Memory hook: babies start with about 300 bones; fusing brings it down to 206.

Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito.
Memory hook: P for Plasmodium, P for Protozoan.

questions.q: The smallest bone in the human body is the:
questions.solution:
The stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear is the smallest bone. The femur (thigh) is the longest.
Memory hook: Stapes is shaped like a tiny stirrup in your ear.

questions.q: Insulin is produced by which organ?
questions.solution:
Insulin is made by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. Its lack causes diabetes.
Memory hook: 'Islets in the Pancreas sea' produce insulin.

questions.q: Which chamber of the human heart pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body through the aorta?
questions.solution:
The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. It has the thickest muscular wall because it pushes blood to the whole body.
Memory hook: the Left ventricle is the Largest pump — thickest wall, sends blood to the whole body.

questions.q: Which of the following diseases is caused by a bacterium?
questions.solution:
Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi. Measles, polio and chickenpox are viral diseases.
Memory hook: Bacterial set 'TCT-TD': TB, Cholera, Typhoid, Tetanus, Diphtheria.
